newsitem.title: GERMANY: BASF, Lynx set up genetic engineering joint-venture.
newsitem.headline: BASF, Lynx set up genetic engineering joint-venture.

text.p: In the first such move of its kind, German chemical group BASF AG is to form a biotechnology and genetic engineering joint-venture with a U.S. company, Lynx Therapeutics, BASF said on Wednesday.

BASF plans to invest over 100 million marks in the joint-venture, which will be based in Heidelberg and will employ around 60 people, BASF management board member Hans-Juergen Quadbeck-Seeger told journalists in Ludwigshafen.

The main activity of the joint-venture, called BASF-Lynx Bioscience AG, will be working with a process developed by Lynx called MPSS, used to analyse genes when researching materials to develop new pesticides and drugs.

Lynx founder Sam Eletr said that with MPSS it is possible to examine the genetic activity of a cell and the joint-venture parties hope to develop an early-warning system against unwanted side-effects from active substances and chemicals.
BASF will hold a 51 percent stake in the joint venture with the Hayward, California-based Lynx group holding a 49 percent stake, BASF said.
Lynx is the first U.S. company to move to Germany to take part in a joint-venture with a German company in the biotechnology and genetic engineering area.
The joint-venture was of strategic importance for BASF, Quadbeck-Seeger, and he said that genetic technology was becoming increasingly accepted in Germany.
Quadbeck-Seeger added that setting up the joint-venture increased the viability of locating genetic technology development projects in Germany on a sound economic basis.
Eletr said that the groups were looking to see how Californian enthusiasm for biotechnology and genetic engineering translated to Germany.

The new company will follow the U.S. practice, common with bio-tech companies there, of allowing employees to buy up to 15 percent of the base capital in the form of non-voting preference shares in the company.
A possible flotation of the company was unlikely earlier than in five years time, Quadbeck-Seeger said.
